turns.t: Right, doc. I've brought my meter and my diary, because I want to understand what's going on. My sugars have been all over the shop.
Good, that's the best way to do it. Let's see the diary. What do you see in the mornings? ~
Mostly high, before breakfast, and then they come down by lunch. Odd, isn't it? ~
Not odd, no. Overnight, your liver puts out sugar. What are you taking for the diabetes at the moment?
Metformin, 500 mg, twice a day, with meals, for my diabetes. And that's it.
Have you got any allergies I should know about?
Penicillin, I think. I know I react to it. I don't remember what happened exactly, I was a kid.
Thank you. Any operations?
A knee operation, a cartilage repair, in 2012.
And any hypos, shaky, sweaty, or feeling faint?
No. None at all.
Good. Looking at the pattern, the morning readings are high, and the daytime ones are mostly fine. Your diabetes isn't as well controlled as I'd like at the moment.
Is it the food? ~
Partly, but the morning highs aren't about breakfast. What do you eat in the evening? ~
A decent dinner, and then a bowl of cereal at ten, with milk. ~
There's the culprit, or one of them. Late-night carbohydrates drive the morning readings. ~
I do love my cereal. ~
I'd suggest dropping the cereal, and having a small protein snack if you're hungry, like a boiled egg or some nuts.
That I can do. ~
And I'd like to increase your metformin to 1000 mg, with your evening meal, and 500 mg with breakfast.
Will it upset my stomach? ~
It can, so take it with food, and we'll go up slowly. ~
Right. ~
Keep testing before breakfast and two hours after your evening meal, and note them down.
Same as now. ~
If your morning readings stay above 10 after two weeks, or you get any readings below 4, call me.
I will. Thanks. Should I still bring the meter to the next visit? ~
Yes, always, it's the most useful thing you can bring. ~
Then I'll see you with it. ~
Good, and well done for keeping such a tidy diary. ~
Thanks, doc. ~
